extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, graduate students, and researchers (especially in geometry/topology)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and informal standards for how to think about, learn, teach, and communicate mathematics (particularly geometry/topology), emphasizing visualization, intuition, and the balance between concise statements and complete proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn ways of thinking rather than memorizing proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: “What mathematicians most wanted and needed from me was to learn my ways of thinking, and not in fact to learn my proof of the geometrization conjecture for Haken manifolds.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize internalizing the approach and viewpoint used to obtain results rather than just recording specific proofs; teaching should aim to transmit modes of thought that students can apply elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand objects by 'living inside' them
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mathematical symbols and even pictures are not sufficient for true understanding, especially in geometry and topology. We must strive to live somehow inside the objects we study, to experience them as 3-dimensional beings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True understanding is experiential and geometric: work to develop an internal, spatial model of the object (beyond formulas or static diagrams) so you can 'encounter' and 'interact' with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and develop visualization skills regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: Thurston attributed his skill to a decision to 'practice visualizing things' every day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate daily practice of mental visualization is recommended as a concrete habit for improving geometric intuition and problem-solving ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphors and vivid imagery to convey core structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples like 'Froth of bubbles. Bounded interaction.' were used to encapsulate complex ideas succinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ short, evocative metaphors or images to communicate central structural ideas; these can guide research and help students focus on the essential intuition behind technical details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value exploratory, live demonstrations in teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Thurston’s lectures often involved drawing, erasing, tinkering and 'delaying things while he quickly thought up the lecture he hadn’t prepared.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spontaneous, exploratory presentations (drawing, manipulating models) can generate insights unavailable through fully prepared lectures; accept temporary disorder if it yields deeper intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise proofs are acceptable provided they are complete and expandable
rubrics_metrics.description: Thurston gave 'complete, albeit concise, proofs' and was 'always willing and able to provide as much detail as I needed, right down to the epsilons.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity in exposition is fine, but authors should ensure correctness and be prepared to supply full epsilon-level details when needed; brevity must not mask gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain correctness; avoid false statements and conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: The author notes Thurston 'never (as far as I can tell) wrote any incorrect statement, or made a conjecture that turned out to be wrong.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for precise, reliable statements and resist speculative claims presented as fact; the standard is to keep published statements correct or clearly labeled as conjectural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of viewpoint is a form of mathematical innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Thurston’s influence included changing the idea of what it means to 'encounter' and 'interact' with mathematical objects; this shift was as important as particular theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing new conceptual frameworks and reframings of problems is a legitimate and high-impact form of contribution; success may be judged by how a viewpoint reshapes a field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical models and constructive representations to realize abstract objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tinker Toy example: for a given Tinker Toy T, the space C(T) of configurations can realize many manifolds; 'every smooth map between manifolds can actually be represented via some rods connecting the two associated tinker toys.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete constructions and toy models can make abstract existence statements and maps tangible; building or visualizing such models is a recommended method to understand and demonstrate results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal explanation and shared insight aids understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The author recalls the 'communal thrill' when Thurston explained how to obtain all compact smooth manifolds from Tinker Toys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group exposition, lively seminars, and sharing of intuitive explanations foster deep understanding that solitary reading may not provide; encourage communal discussion and demonstration.
